display_name: NATO-side emitters, receivers and jammers of the 1980s, and each side's threat library
status: E1 data set (October 2026). Band and year facts come from public encyclopaedic pages (tier 4: for NATO equipment these are the operator-country reference tier available online); everything numeric that no source gives (power, gain, sensitivity, bearing accuracy, PRF windows) is a labelled estimate of the system CLASS from the textbooks in docs/SOURCES.md, not a measurement of a particular set. Sources that were not reachable (US Army FM 100-2-3, Soviet and NATO threat handbooks) are listed in docs/research/EM_E1_NATO_DATA_2026-10.md with what to read for.
notes: Used with data/em/osa_ak.json: the red ESM library 'red_esm_nato_view' is what the Warsaw Pact side believed about NATO emitters; the blue RWR library 'blue_rwr_nato_view' is what NATO believed about Soviet ones (including the SA-8). Both are beliefs, deliberately wider than the truth.

sources.title: Encyclopaedic pages: AN/APG-63 (X band, in service 1973 on the F-15A/B), AN/APG-66 (X band 6.2-10.9 GHz; mechanically scanned; ±10/30/60 deg; low PRF uplook, medium PRF downlook; 80 nmi), P-19 'Flat Face B' (UHF 830-875 MHz, 900 kW, 360 deg, 260 km, 1974)
sources.notes: Wikipedia. Read 11 Oct 2026; no power or PRF values are given for the APG-63/66, so those are estimates.

sources.title: Encyclopaedic pages: AN/ALR-46 RWR (2-18 GHz; flown in Southeast Asia from January 1973), AN/ALQ-99 tactical jamming system (10 bands from 64 MHz to 20 GHz; band 8 4-7.8 GHz, band 9 7.8-11 GHz, band 10 11-20 GHz; three under-wing transmit pods and a tail receive pod; maximum output 10.8 kW older, 6.8 kW newer; AN/ALQ-99A 1972; EA-6B, EF-111A)
D. Adamy, EW 101 and EW 102 (Artech); R. Wiley, ELINT (Artech); D. Schleher, Electronic Warfare in the Information Age: class values for receiver sensitivity, bearing accuracy, ERP and PRF ranges
sources.notes: Used only for labelled estimates of a system class.

threat_libraries.name: What NATO RWRs believed about Soviet emitters
threat_libraries.notes: Bands from Western references. Wider than the truth on purpose. PRF and pulse width are not constrained: not public.

threat_libraries.name: What the Warsaw Pact side believed about NATO emitters
threat_libraries.notes: Bands from the NATO equipment's public descriptions. A Czechoslovak 1985 analysis expected every newly switched-on source to be located within seconds (vr_1985_plss); this is the library such a station would match against.
